A.explanation: This is $\text{J s}^{-1}$ which equals the watt, but the joule $\text{J}$ is a derived unit, not an SI base unit.

B.explanation: Power is energy per time, which expands fully to $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-3}$, using only base units kg, m and s.

C.explanation: This has $\text{s}^{-1}$ instead of $\text{s}^{-3}$, so it is missing division by $\text{s}^{2}$ from force and energy.

D.explanation: This is $\text{N m s}^{-1}$ which equals the watt, but the newton $\text{N}$ is a derived unit, not an SI base unit.

hints: Notice the question asks for SI base units, so answers containing $\text{J}$ or $\text{N}$ cannot be accepted even though they equal the watt.
Start from power as rate of energy transfer: $P = W/t$ in $\text{J s}^{-1}$, then recall $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m}$.
Expand force using $F = ma$ to get $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$, then combine the extra $\text{m}$ and the extra $\text{s}^{-1}$ for power.
walkthrough: Identify the watt: power $P$ is work done or energy transferred per unit time, so $P = W/t$ with unit $\text{J s}^{-1}$.
Expand the joule: work $W = Fs$, so $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m} = 1 \text{ N} \times 1 \text{ m}$.
Expand the newton: from $F = ma$, $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$.
Substitute back: $1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J s}^{-1} = (1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2} \times 1 \text{ m}) \times 1 \text{ s}^{-1} = 1 \text{ kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-3}$.
Check units: only $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$ and $\text{s}$ remain, which are SI base units. This is option B.
